card.h1: The Tale of Kiều: Nguyễn Du and the Poem That Became a Nation
A country that tells its fortune with a poem

ul.li: 3,254 lines of verse, written in chữ Nôm, completed before the poet's death in 1820
Readers who could not read the script held long stretches of it by memory, and it was recited rather than only studied
It generated its own folk practices: bói Kiều (opening the book at random to divine one's fate), lẩy Kiều and tập Kiều (quoting and recombining its lines)
Scholar Phạm Quỳnh, 1924: "So long as The Tale of Kiều survives, our language survives; so long as our language survives, our country survives."

The argument of this lecture (a reading, not a documented fact): Nguyễn Du took a minor Chinese prose romance, retold it in a folk meter, and gave a woman sold into prostitution a sustained inner voice — and Vietnamese readers have read their own history through her since

card.h1: I. The poet
He lived through the fall of the Lê, the fall of the Tây Sơn, and the founding of the Nguyễn

ul.li: Born 1765 in Thăng Long (Hanoi); courtesy name Tố Như, art name Thanh Hiên
His father, Nguyễn Nghiễm, reached the highest ranks of the Lê court; the family had served at the top of the state for generations
Orphaned at thirteen: father died 1776, mother 1778, and the household dispersed

The chronology, exactly: Tây Sơn forces took the northern capital in 1786 to 1788; the Later Lê dynasty ended in 1789. The Tây Sơn were defeated in turn, and the Nguyễn dynasty was founded in 1802, lasting until 1945
Two dynasties fell in his lifetime, not three: he died in 1820, eighteen years into the Nguyễn
After 1788 he spent what he called his "ten years of wind and dust," poor and without office

card.h1: He took office under the dynasty that replaced the one his family served

ul.li: 1802: Gia Long founds the Nguyễn dynasty, having defeated the Tây Sơn, not the Lê, whose line had already ended in 1789
He is appointed a district magistrate: a man raised in Lê service now administering for the new house
1804: he pleads illness and resigns, is summoned back, and is promoted repeatedly
1813: sent to Qing China as chief tribute envoy; returns with Bắc hành tạp lục, whose poems dwell on history's wronged and forgotten
Dies in 1820, before a second mission

How far to press the parallel: the poem's central problem, keeping faith when survival requires breaking it, has an evident resemblance to his position. We have no record of his daily motives, so treat the resemblance as a reading of the poem, not as evidence of why he wrote it

card.h1: II. The making of the poem
What Nguyễn Du did to his Chinese source

ul.li: The source: Jin Yun Qiao (Vietnamese: Kim Vân Kiều truyện), a 17th-century Chinese prose romance by a writer using the pen name Qingxin Caizi, "Pure-Hearted Man of Talent"
He kept the characters, the sequence of events, and the moral frame

Scholars disagree on how much he altered. Đào Duy Anh judged that he "preserved the Chinese story without cutting or adding anything"; other accounts of the same comparison note that he dropped material, redistributed it, and compressed long passages into a few lines. Both readings agree the plot is inherited; they disagree on the scale of the pruning
Where he spent his length: the closing reunion runs 526 lines, about one sixth of the poem
Interpretation: the shift is from plot to psychology. The events are borrowed; the sustained interiority is his

card.h1: He also made it Vietnamese, not merely translated

ul.li: Written in chữ Nôm, the demotic script for the Vietnamese language, at a time when Literary Chinese ran the state and carried prestige
Cast in lục bát, the native folk meter, rather than a Tang-derived form
Saturated with Vietnamese proverbs, idioms, and everyday speech; the landscapes and social textures read as Vietnamese despite the nominal Ming-dynasty Chinese setting
The setting is dated within the poem itself: "Rằng năm Gia Tĩnh triều Minh", the Jiajing reign of the Ming, lines 9 to 10
A work in the people's script and the people's meter could circulate as common property rather than court property

card.h1: The poem states its thesis in its opening couplets
card.p:
Trăm năm trong cõi người ta,
Chữ tài chữ mệnh khéo là ghét nhau.
Trải qua một cuộc bể dâu,
Những điều trông thấy mà đau đớn lòng.
(lines 1 to 4)

ul.li: Literal gloss: a hundred years within the realm of humankind, and the words tài (talent) and mệnh (destiny) are skilled at hating each other
Tài mệnh tương đố: the traditional doctrine that gifts attract the hostility of fate. The poem announces its argument before its story

Bể dâu, from bãi bể nương dâu ("sea-bed into mulberry field"), is a classical figure for total upheaval. Whether readers in 1820 heard recent dynastic collapse in it is a common critical inference, not a documented reception
Line 4 commits the poet to a stance: what he has seen hurts (đau đớn lòng). The humanitarian argument follows from that verb

card.h1: III. The story
The vow, and the price of a daughter

ul.li: Kiều, her sister Thúy Vân, and their brother Vương Quan visit the graves at the spring festival. Kiều weeps at the tomb of Đạm Tiên, a dead singing-girl as gifted and as unlucky as herself; the poem plants her fate in its first episode
She meets the young scholar Kim Trọng and they exchange a private vow of marriage; he leaves to mourn an uncle
A false accusation ruins the family and puts her father and brother in danger of prison; money is what the officials want
Kiều sells herself in marriage to raise it, and asks Thúy Vân to take her place in the betrothal to Kim
Nguyễn Du writes the sale as a haggle: "Cò kè bớt một thêm hai", a bit off and a bit on, until the price settles at "vàng ngoài bốn trăm", just over four hundred in gold

card.h1: Fifteen years of being bought and sold

ul.li: Mã Giám Sinh, the buyer, is a procurer. He violates her and delivers her to Tú Bà's brothel; she refuses clients and attempts suicide
Tú Bà hires the confidence man Sở Khanh to stage an elopement and betray it, a deliberate operation to break her will. Kiều submits
Thúc Sinh buys her out and marries her; his first wife Hoạn Thư, a minister's daughter, has her abducted, made a household servant, and forced to wait at their table
She escapes to the nun Giác Duyên, is passed on for safety, and is trafficked into a second brothel
Từ Hải, a rebel commander, marries her and establishes his own domain; she holds court and judges the people who wronged her

card.h1: The state is the last and worst betrayer

ul.li: The imperial commissioner Hồ Tôn Hiến offers amnesty. Kiều, persuaded and wanting a legitimate life, urges Từ Hải to accept
The amnesty is a trap. Từ Hải's forces are attacked and he is killed, after his wife's advice
Hồ Tôn Hiến forces her to perform at his victory banquet, desires her, and marries her off to a minor local official to avoid scandal
She throws herself into the Qiantang River (Vietnamese: sông Tiền Đường). Giác Duyên, forewarned, is waiting with nets
Interpretation to press in discussion: her final ruin is administered not by a pimp or a jealous wife but by the emperor's lawful representative

card.h1: A reunion that refuses to be a happy ending

ul.li: Kim Trọng has married Thúy Vân as Kiều asked, entered office, provided for her parents, and searched for her
He finds her living with Giác Duyên. The family is restored and the marriage is finally performed
Kiều declines the marriage bed. They live as companions, honoring the vow of their youth without consummating it
Nguyễn Du gives this settlement about one sixth of the poem, more space than any single disaster receives
For discussion: restoration, or the poem conceding that fifteen years cannot be repaid? The refusal is hers, and the text does not explain it away

card.h1: IV. The two values
Thúy Kiều is built out of specific textual detail, not summary

ul.li: Her gifts are itemized on introduction: poetry and painting, song, the five-note scale, and mastery of the hồ cầm, a stringed instrument usually Englished as lute or fiddle, lines 29 to 32
Her own composition is named Bạc mệnh, "thin destiny," and the text says it grieves whoever hears it, line 34. Her art is introduced as an omen rather than an accomplishment
Her beauty is described through competition: "Hoa ghen thua thắm, liễu hờn kém xanh", flowers envious and willows resentful, line 26
Her bind is a collision of duties rather than melodrama: hiếu (filial obligation) against tình (her vow to Kim). The poem supplies no clean resolution
She soliloquizes at each sale, so the narration stays inside her reasoning, shame, and self-justification. She is also permitted to be wrong: the surrender she counsels destroys Từ Hải

card.h1: Realistic value: every turn of the plot is a transaction

ul.li: "Một ngày lạ thói sai nha / Làm cho khốc hại chẳng qua vì tiền": the bailiffs' cruelty comes down to money
"Trong tay đã sẵn đồng tiền / Dầu lòng đổi trắng thay đen khó gì": with money in hand, turning white into black is no hard thing
"Tiền lưng đã sẵn việc gì chẳng xong": with cash in the purse, what business does not get done?
Follow the money through the plot: money ruins her father, a purchase enslaves her, a purchase frees her, and an official's calculation kills her husband
The indictment is institutional, not incidental: courts, merchants, and the imperial commission are all shown to be purchasable, and Mã Giám Sinh and Sở Khanh are educated men working as traffickers

card.h1: Humanitarian value: he defends a woman his society would condemn

ul.li: Neo-Confucian orthodoxy measured a woman's worth by chữ trinh, chastity. Kiều is sold into brothels twice, and the conventional verdict is ruin
The poem's counter-argument: virtue is intention under coercion, not bodily condition. She sold herself for her father and kept the vow in her heart

His sympathy runs wider than his heroine: to Đạm Tiên, an entertainer nobody mourns; to Từ Hải, whom the state calls a bandit and the poem treats as a hero; even Hoạn Thư is given a defense at her trial shrewd enough that Kiều releases her
The near-closing couplet, lines 3251 to 3252: "Thiện căn ở tại lòng ta / Chữ tâm kia mới bằng ba chữ tài", the root of good lies in our own heart, and the word tâm is worth three times the word tài
Just before it, lines 3247 to 3248 turn the thesis into a pun: "Có tài mà cậy chi tài / Chữ tài liền với chữ tai một vần", tài (talent) rhymes with tai (disaster)

card.h1: V. The art of lục bát
How the six-eight line works, in the lines we just read

ul.li: Structure: couplets alternating a six-syllable line with an eight-syllable line, beginning on six and ending on eight. Kiều is 1,627 such couplets
The chain rhyme, demonstrated on lines 1 to 6. Line 1 ends ta, which rhymes with the sixth syllable of line 2, là (Chữ tài chữ mệnh khéo là ghét nhau): a waist rhyme, yêu vận, landing inside the line
Line 2 ends nhau, picked up by dâu at the end of line 3, whose rhyme then sits at the sixth syllable of line 4, đau (Những điều trông thấy mà đau đớn lòng)

Line 4 ends lòng, which carries into the next couplet: "Lạ gì bỉ sắc tư phong, / Trời xanh quen thói má hồng đánh ghen", lines 5 to 6, where phong closes the six-line and hồng is the sixth syllable of the eight

Tones: syllables 2, 4, and 6 run bằng, trắc, bằng, by the rule "nhất, tam, ngũ bất luận": in line 2, tài, mệnh, là. Syllables 6 and 8 of the long line are both bằng but must differ in tone: là (huyền) against nhau (ngang)

card.h1: Why the form suits this story

ul.li: It is the meter of ca dao and lullabies, and Vietnam's folk-poetry tradition is composed almost entirely in it
Unlike court forms, it was composed and enjoyed across every class

Structural consequence: the interlocking rhyme has no stanza break and no terminal stop, so each couplet hands off to the next. Interpretation: the form unspools, which suits a life sliding from one disaster into the next
Practical consequence: a chain-rhymed folk meter is memorable, which is part of why the poem circulated by recitation
Choosing this meter for a 3,254-line narrative put the poem in the same register as the songs its audience already knew

card.h1: What English cannot carry: four translators, one opening

ul.li: Vladislav Zhukov (2004) keeps a formal meter: "Were full five-score the years allotted to born man"
Timothy Allen (2019) abandons meter for voice: "It's an old story: good luck and good looks / don't always mix."
Nguyễn Bình (2021) chooses the English heroic couplet: "'Tween Fate and Talent hatred seems to reign."
Huỳnh Sanh Thông (1983, Yale) blank verse remains the standard scholarly English version, and the poem exists in roughly twenty languages

What resists translation is the prosody rather than the imagery: no English meter reproduces a tonal waist rhyme, so each translator sacrifices music, compression, or plainness. Discuss the differences in paraphrase rather than by quoting at length

card.h1: The afterlife of a poem

ul.li: Adapted into cải lương and chèo opera, painting, and Western-style opera; Kim Vân Kiều (1924) is described as the first feature film made in Vietnam
Under French rule it was recruited as evidence that Vietnamese was a literary language, then reinterpreted in turn by North, South, and the unified state
American officials have quoted it at Vietnamese counterparts: President Clinton in Hanoi in 2000, Vice President Joe Biden in Washington in July 2015, and President Obama in Hanoi in 2016

Biden's couplet, at a State Department lunch for Party General Secretary Nguyễn Phú Trọng: "Trời còn để có hôm nay / Tan sương đầu ngõ vén mây giữa trời", heaven has granted us this day; the mist at the lane's end clears and the clouds part

Clinton chose lines on the turn of the seasons: "Sen tàn cúc lại nở hoa / Sầu dài ngày ngắn đông đà sang xuân". The English renderings used on these occasions are reported to come from Huỳnh Sanh Thông's translation
Vietnam marked his 250th birth anniversary in 2015 as a national commemoration, with UNESCO taking part

card.h1: Nguyễn Du expected to be forgotten

ul.li: The actual final couplet, lines 3253 to 3254: "Lời quê chắp nhặt dông dài / Mua vui cũng được một vài trống canh", rustic words strung together at length, good for a few hours' amusement
The tâm and tài couplet is the penultimate statement, lines 3251 to 3252; this self-deprecating envoi follows it and closes the poem
The modesty was a convention of the form. The estimate was wrong: the poem became oracle, national symbol, and diplomatic language

What the lecture has argued: he inherited a plot and supplied a consciousness; he wrote in the people's script and the people's meter; and he held that a woman sold twice into a brothel had kept her honor
The claim that still reads plainly: tâm outweighs tài, what you intend outweighs what you are gifted with

brief.instruction: Academic register for a university literature audience: precise, confident, and specific, with no promotional adjectives and no hedging filler. Assume an intelligent audience with no prior knowledge of Vietnamese literature: define Vietnamese terms at first use and never assume the plot is known. Target about 55 words per slide; the template holds median 55, p90 81, so budget 55 and go to 81 only on a deliberately text-only slide such as the prosody demonstration or the translation comparison. Write claims, not topic labels: every bullet should assert something a listener could learn from or dispute, and carry a name, number, date, line number, or quotation where one exists. Prefer the concrete instance to the general statement. Vary sentence and paragraph length. Do not use the "Bold term: explanation" pattern as a slide's default structure; the bold lead-ins already in the outline are deliberate and sufficient. No signposting, no sweeping openers, no summary or inspirational closers, none of the "not just X, it's Y" contrast family, and no em dashes in generated prose. Vietnamese diacritics must be reproduced exactly as written in the outline: Nguyễn Du, Thúy Kiều, Truyện Kiều, lục bát, chữ Nôm, Từ Hải, Hoạn Thư, Đạm Tiên, Tiền Đường, hồ cầm, tài, mệnh, tâm. A missing or wrong diacritic is a factual error in this deck. Keep Vietnamese quotations in Vietnamese with the English gloss adjacent, and never silently replace a Vietnamese line with its translation.

This deck is a corrected lecture, and its credibility rests on three registers being kept apart in the writing. Do not blur them. 1. Documented fact: dates, line numbers, quoted text, named sources. Reproduce these exactly as the outline gives them and never round, upgrade, or embellish. Do not add a figure, date, price, or superlative that is not in the outline, and do not restore ones an earlier draft carried: there is no "three hundred taels" demand, no stated span of years for Từ Hải's domain, and no count of memorized lines attributed to named groups of readers. 2. Interpretation: readings of the poem, including the lecture's own argument. Introduce these as readings ("the poem treats", "on this reading", "for discussion"), never as established fact. The outline already marks them; keep the marking in the finished copy. 3. Illustrative or inferred material: critical inferences about reception, resemblances between the poet's life and his plot. Say that they are inferences, as the outline does. Forbidden claim types in this deck: any "first ever", "earliest", or "only" claim about Vietnamese literature or about Kiều as a character; any statement about Nguyễn Du's private motives or daily feelings; any claim that Gia Long overthrew the Lê. The Lê line ended in 1789, the Tây Sơn were defeated in 1802, the Nguyễn dynasty ran 1802 to 1945, and Nguyễn Du died in 1820, so two dynasties fell within his lifetime. Quoted translation excerpts stay short, a line or two, and always carry the translator's name. Extended discussion of a translation is paraphrase, not quotation. Do not introduce anecdotes, quotations, or examples that are not in this outline.

Sustain the template's authored look exactly: pressed-paper ground, thin inset frames and hairline rules, one dark accent for emphasis and Roman numerals, book serif throughout. This is a lecture deck that must stay legible on a projector, so favor generous margins, restrained type sizes, and high text contrast over decorative density. Imagery is period and documentary in register, natural color, never illustrative kitsch: chữ Nôm woodblock pages and manuscript leaves, brush calligraphy, aged paper and book bindings, stringed instruments of the hồ cầm family, northern Vietnamese landscapes in directional light (river mist, limestone, temple architecture, lotus), and literary portraiture or memorial statuary. No modern people, no readable English text in images, no logos, no cartoon or watercolor-storybook treatment. Give the five chapter dividers the template's Roman-numeral act treatment with full-field photography and no body text. Three slides earn a substantial visual treatment rather than a picture. The opening-couplets slide sets the Vietnamese verse as a typographic pull-quote with the gloss subordinate and the line numbers visible. The prosody slide needs a real diagram built from the exact quoted text, lines 1 to 6: mark the rhyme links ta to là, nhau to dâu, dâu to đau, and lòng to phong to hồng, with syllable positions numbered 1 to 6 and 1 to 8 so each waist rhyme is visibly the sixth syllable, and label bằng and trắc at positions 2, 4, 6, and 8. The diagram must contain no syllable that does not appear in those six lines. The translation slide is a ruled lane table, one lane per translator, with the translator's name in each lane. Elsewhere use roughly one image every second or third slide. The two plot slides covering fifteen years can carry more structure than usual, since they track a sequence of sales and betrayals.
